{{Short description|Set of random variables of which any two are independent}}
In [[probability theory]], a '''pairwise independent''' collection of [[random variable]]s is a set of random variables any two of which are [[statistical independence|independent]].<ref>Gut, A. (2005) ''Probability: a Graduate Course'', Springer-Verlag. {{isbn|0-387-27332-8}}. pp.&nbsp;71&ndash;72.</ref>  Any collection of [[Mutual independence|mutually independent]] random variables is pairwise independent, but some pairwise independent collections are not mutually independent.  Pairwise independent random variables with finite [[variance]] are [[uncorrelated]].

A pair of random variables ''X'' and ''Y'' are '''independent''' [[if and only if]] the random vector (''X'', ''Y'') with [[joint distribution|joint]] [[cumulative distribution function]] (CDF) <math>F_{X,Y}(x,y)</math> satisfies

<math display="block">F_{X,Y}(x,y) = F_X(x) F_Y(y),</math>

or equivalently, their joint density <math>f_{X,Y}(x,y)</math> satisfies

<math display="block">f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_X(x) f_Y(y).</math>

That is, the joint distribution is equal to the product of the marginal distributions.<ref>{{cite book|title=Introduction to Mathematical Statistics|author = Hogg, R. V., McKean, J. W., Craig, A. T.| edition=6| year=2005| publisher=Pearson Prentice Hall|location=Upper Saddle River, NJ|isbn=0-13-008507-3}} Definition 2.5.1, page 109.</ref>

Unless it is not clear in context, in practice the modifier "mutual" is usually dropped so that '''independence''' means '''mutual independence'''. A statement such as " ''X'', ''Y'', ''Z'' are independent random variables" means that ''X'', ''Y'', ''Z'' are mutually independent.

==Example==

Pairwise independence does not imply mutual independence, as shown by the following example attributed to S. Bernstein.<ref>{{cite book|title=Introduction to Mathematical Statistics|author = Hogg, R. V., McKean, J. W., Craig, A. T.| edition=6| year=2005| publisher=Pearson Prentice Hall|location=Upper Saddle River, NJ|isbn=0-13-008507-3}} Remark 2.6.1, p. 120.</ref>

Suppose ''X'' and ''Y'' are two independent tosses of a [[fair coin]], where we designate 1 for heads and 0 for tails. Let the third random variable ''Z'' be equal to 1 if exactly one of those coin tosses resulted in "heads", and 0 otherwise (i.e., <math>Z = X \oplus Y</math>). Then jointly the triple (''X'', ''Y'', ''Z'') has the following [[joint probability distribution|probability distribution]]:

<math display="block">(X,Y,Z) = \begin{cases}
(0,0,0) & \text{with probability}\ 1/4, \\
(0,1,1) & \text{with probability}\ 1/4, \\
(1,0,1) & \text{with probability}\ 1/4, \\
(1,1,0) & \text{with probability}\ 1/4.
\end{cases}</math>

Here the [[marginal probability distribution]]s are identical: <math>f_X(0) = f_Y(0) = f_Z(0) = 1/2,</math> and
<math>f_X(1) = f_Y(1) = f_Z(1) = 1/2.</math> The [[bivariate distribution]]s also agree: <math> f_{X,Y} = f_{X,Z} = f_{Y,Z}, </math> where <math>f_{X,Y}(0,0)=f_{X,Y}(0,1)=f_{X,Y}(1,0)=f_{X,Y}(1,1)=1/4.</math>

Since each of the pairwise joint distributions equals the product of their respective marginal distributions, the variables are pairwise independent:

* ''X'' and ''Y'' are independent, and
* ''X'' and ''Z'' are independent, and
* ''Y'' and ''Z'' are independent.

However, ''X'', ''Y'', and ''Z'' are '''not''' [[Mutually_independent#More_than_two_random_variables|mutually independent]], since <math>f_{X,Y,Z}(x,y,z) \neq f_X(x)f_Y(y)f_Z(z),</math> the left side equalling for example 1/4 for (''x'', ''y'', ''z'') = (0, 0, 0) while the right side equals 1/8 for (''x'', ''y'', ''z'') = (0, 0, 0). In fact, any of <math>\{X,Y,Z\}</math> is completely determined by the other two (any of ''X'', ''Y'', ''Z'' is the [[modular arithmetic|sum (modulo 2)]] of the others). That is as far from independence as random variables can get.

==Probability of the union of pairwise independent events ==
Bounds on the [[probability]] that the sum of [[Bernoulli distribution|Bernoulli]] [[random variables]] is at least one, commonly known as the [[Boole's inequality|union bound]], are provided by the [[Fréchet inequalities|Boole–Fréchet]]<ref name=boole54>Boole, G. (1854). ''An Investigation of the Laws of Thought, On Which Are Founded the Mathematical Theories of Logic and Probability.'' Walton and Maberly, London. See Boole's "major" and "minor" limits of a conjunction on page 299.</ref><ref name=frechet35>Fréchet, M. (1935). Généralisations du théorème des probabilités totales. ''Fundamenta Mathematicae'' '''25''': 379–387.</ref> inequalities. While these bounds assume only [[univariate]] information, several bounds with knowledge of general [[Joint probability distribution|bivariate]] probabilities, have been proposed too. Denote by <math>\{{A}_i, i \in \{1,2,...,n\}\}</math> a set of  <math>n</math>  [[Bernoulli distribution|Bernoulli]] events with [[probability]] of occurrence <math>\mathbb{P}(A_{i})=p_i</math>  for each <math>i</math>. Suppose the [[Joint probability distribution|bivariate]] probabilities are given by <math>\mathbb{P}(A_{i} \cap A_{j})=p_{ij}</math> for every pair of indices <math>(i,j)</math>. Kounias <ref name="Kounias">{{cite journal|journal=The Annals of Mathematical Statistics|volume=39|pages= 2154–2158|year=1968|author=E. G. Kounias|title=Bounds for the probability of a union, with applications|issue=6 |doi=10.1214/aoms/1177698049 |doi-access=free}}</ref> derived the following [[Upper and lower bounds|upper bound]]:
<math display="block">
 \mathbb{P}(\displaystyle {\cup}_iA_{i}) \leq \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n p_{i}-\underset {j\in \{1,2,..,n\}}{\max} \sum_{i\neq j} p_{ij},
</math>
which subtracts the maximum weight of a [[Star (graph theory)|star]] [[spanning tree]] on a [[complete graph]] with <math>n</math> nodes (where the edge weights are given by <math>p_{ij}</math>) from the sum of the [[Marginal distribution|marginal]] probabilities <math>\sum_i p_i</math>. <br>
Hunter-Worsley<ref name="Hunter">{{cite journal|journal=Journal of Applied Probability|volume=13|number=3|pages= 597–603|year=1976|author=D. Hunter|title=An upper bound for the probability of a union|doi=10.2307/3212481 |jstor=3212481 }}</ref><ref name="Worsley">{{cite journal|journal=Biometrika|volume=69|number=2|pages= 297–302|year=1982|author=K. J. Worsley|title=An improved Bonferroni inequality and applications|doi=10.1093/biomet/69.2.297 }}</ref> tightened this [[Upper and lower bounds|upper bound]] by optimizing over <math>\tau \in T</math> as follows:
<math display="block">
\mathbb{P}(\displaystyle {\cup}_i A_{i}) \leq \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n p_{i}-\underset {\tau \in T}{\max}\sum_{(i,j) \in \tau} p_{ij},
</math>
where <math>T</math> is the set of all [[Spanning tree|spanning trees]] on the graph. These bounds are not the [[Upper and lower bounds#Tight bounds|tightest]] possible with general [[Joint probability distribution|bivariates]] <math>p_{ij}</math> even when [[Feasible region|feasibility]] is guaranteed as shown in Boros et.al.<ref name="Boros2014">{{cite journal
| last1=Boros | first1=Endre | authorlink1=Endre Boros
| last2=Scozzari | first2=Andrea
| last3=Tardella | first3=Fabio
| last4=Veneziani | first4=Pierangela
| title=Polynomially computable bounds for the probability of the union of events
| journal=[[Mathematics of Operations Research]]
| volume=39
| number=4
| pages=1311–1329
| date=2014
| doi=10.1287/moor.2014.0657}}</ref> However, when the variables are [[#Example|pairwise independent]] (<math>p_{ij}=p_ip_j</math>), Ramachandra—Natarajan <ref name=Ramachandra-Natarajan>{{cite journal
| last1=Ramachandra | first1=Arjun Kodagehalli
| last2=Natarajan | first2=Karthik
| title=Tight Probability Bounds with Pairwise Independence
| journal=SIAM Journal on Discrete Mathematics
| volume=37
| issue=2
| pages=516–555
| date=2023
| arxiv=2006.00516
| doi=10.1137/21M140829}}</ref> showed that the Kounias-Hunter-Worsley <ref name="Kounias">{{cite journal|journal=The Annals of Mathematical Statistics|volume=39|pages= 2154–2158|year=1968|author=E. G. Kounias|title=Bounds for the probability of a union, with applications|issue=6 |doi=10.1214/aoms/1177698049 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Hunter">{{cite journal|journal=Journal of Applied Probability|volume=13|number=3|pages= 597–603|year=1976|author=D. Hunter|title=An upper bound for the probability of a union|doi=10.2307/3212481 |jstor=3212481 }}</ref><ref name="Worsley">{{cite journal|journal=Biometrika|volume=69|number=2|pages= 297–302|year=1982|author=K. J. Worsley|title=An improved Bonferroni inequality and applications|doi=10.1093/biomet/69.2.297 }}</ref> bound is [[Upper and lower bounds#Tight bounds|tight]] by proving that the maximum probability of the union of events admits a [[closed-form expression]] given as:

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\max \mathbb{P}(\displaystyle {\cup}_i A_{i})  =  \displaystyle \min\left(\sum_{i=1}^n p_i - p_n \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} p_{i}\right),1\right)</math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}

where the [[Probability|probabilities]] are sorted in increasing order as <math> 0 \leq p_1 \leq p_2 \leq \ldots \leq p_n \leq 1</math>. The [[Upper and lower bounds#Tight bounds|tight]] bound in {{EquationNote|1|Eq. 1}} depends only on the sum of the smallest <math>n-1</math> [[Probability|probabilities]] <math>\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} p_{i}</math> and the largest probability <math>p_n</math>. Thus, while [[Sorting|ordering]] of the [[Probability|probabilities]] plays a role in the derivation of the bound, the [[Sorting|ordering]] among the smallest <math>n-1</math> [[Probability|probabilities]] <math>\{p_1,p_2,\dots,p_{n-1}\}</math> is inconsequential since only their sum is used.

===Comparison with the [[Fréchet inequalities|Boole–Fréchet]] [[Boole's inequality|union bound]]===
It is useful to compare the smallest bounds on the probability of the union with arbitrary [[Dependent and independent variables|dependence]] and [[#Example|pairwise independence]] respectively. The [[Upper and lower bounds#Tight bounds|tightest]] [[Fréchet inequalities|Boole–Fréchet]] [[Upper and lower bounds|upper]] [[Boole's inequality|union bound]] (assuming only [[univariate]] information) is given as:<br>
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">
 \displaystyle \max \mathbb{P}(\displaystyle {\cup}_i A_{i}) = \displaystyle \min\left(\sum_{i=1}^n p_{i},1\right)
</math>|{{EquationRef|2}}}}
As shown in Ramachandra-Natarajan,<ref name=Ramachandra-Natarajan></ref> it can be easily verified that the ratio of the two [[Upper and lower bounds#Tight bounds|tight]] bounds in {{EquationNote|2|Eq. 2}} and {{EquationNote|1|Eq. 1}} is [[Upper and lower bounds|upper bounded]] by <math>4/3</math> where the maximum value of <math>4/3</math> is attained when
<math display="block">\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} p_i = 1/2 \, , \quad p_n=1/2</math>
where the [[Probability|probabilities]] are sorted in increasing order as <math> 0 \leq p_1 \leq p_2 \leq \dots \leq p_n \leq 1</math>. In other words, in the best-case scenario, the pairwise independence bound in {{EquationNote|1|Eq. 1}} provides an improvement of <math>25\%</math> over the [[univariate]] bound in {{EquationNote|2|Eq. 2}}.

==Generalization==

More generally, we can talk about ''k''-wise independence, for any ''k''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;2. The idea is similar: a set of [[random variable]]s is ''k''-wise independent if every subset of size ''k'' of those variables is independent. ''k''-wise independence has been used in theoretical computer science, where it was used to prove a theorem about the problem [[MAXEkSAT]].

''k''-wise independence is used in the proof that [[k-independent hashing]] functions are secure unforgeable [[message authentication code]]s.
